source.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
source.authors: Sekh Mainul Islam; Pepa Atanasova; Isabelle Augenstein

record.tranche_reason: The study measures personalization-related polysemanticity with k-sparse probes, a different measure from counting poles with one main job. Its comparison of MoE and dense models bears on V2, but it does not estimate the claimed shares of interpretable neuron poles.
record.gate_note: The study reports k-sparse probe results and automated explanations of crosscoder latents, not percentages of neuron poles with one or more jobs. The explanation results concern learned latents rather than neurons. It also reports several results about latent-to-expert mapping and causal patching; the included patching rows record the reported sufficiency result, not a test of attribution graphs built from neurons.
record.test_reason: The study does not estimate the share of neuron poles with one main job in any model. Its k-sparse probe compares how well few neurons decode 20 personalization concepts in MoE versus dense models. That is decodability, not an audit of what each neuron does, so it is a related but different construct. It also takes dense polysemanticity as a premise rather than testing it. The explanation scoring is applied to crosscoder latents, not neurons, so it cannot bear on V6 or V7. The patching tests crosscoder latents, not neuron attribution graphs, so it cannot bear on V5. The probe finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that personalized MoEs match or beat dense models with similar active parameters while using about 20% of total parameters. They add that the latents map onto stable, distinct experts (Qwen3: S=0.81, D=0.94), and that boosting those experts moves the non-personalized model toward the personalized one. They call the probe results evidence of 'monosemantic behavior of MoE experts for personalization'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses k-sparse probing of personalization concepts and crosscoder-latent analysis rather than counting explained neuron poles or testing pole explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe results are reported across k values from 64 to 1; the study identifies the best-performing layer/component. It notes that selecting among more MoE candidates may favor MoEs and that selection effects may remain, particularly at k = 1. Crosscoder analyses use one selected layer per model.

fits_no_version.finding: For 20 personalization concepts, k-sparse probes on routed tokens of the best MoE expert reach higher balanced accuracy than probes on the best MLP of dense models with matched active parameters. The gap persists at k=1, but selection over more MoE candidates may inflate it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single neurons in MoE experts decode personalization concepts better than single neurons in dense models of matched active size.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM-scored explanations of personalized crosscoder latents reach F1 of 0.63–0.70 overall and 0.81–0.88 in the top activation bin.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-based explanations of SAE/crosscoder latents mainly describe strong activations and predict weak ones less well.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding personalized-latent decoder contributions reduces KL to the personalized model more than random or shared latents do.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Crosscoder latents that are specific to fine-tuning are sufficient to recover much of the fine-tuned behaviour.

record.problems: The probe uses token-level labels for concepts defined over whole responses, which the authors say introduces label noise. They select the best of many components, which may favor MoEs; selection effects may remain, particularly at k = 1. The study analyzes one layer per model and only a controlled, English, group-preference personalization setting. Crosscoder reconstruction is imperfect, with fractions of variance explained of 0.80 for OLMoE, 0.74 for Qwen3-30B-A3B, and 0.65 for Mixtral. Several plotted probe and causal-patching values are not numerically stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The plotted k-sparse-probe trajectories for k = 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, and 2 in Figure 3 were not separately extracted: the text gives the qualitative comparison and highlights k = 1, but the other plotted values are not stated numerically. Other plotted values for latent patching and steering in Figures 10 and 17 were not extracted where the text did not state a numerical outcome.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of the one-job, two-job and not-understood shares.
No pole-share estimates in any model. The MoE–dense probe comparison measures concept decodability, not shares of single-job neurons.
No vision models and no reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No measure of how interpretable-neuron shares change with tools or architecture. The authors say architecture cannot be separated from training differences.
No neuron-based attribution graphs; the patching uses crosscoder latents.
Explanations are of crosscoder latents, not neurons.
Scoring is of crosscoder latents, not neurons, and no share of well-scored neurons is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The study's premise, that dense neurons are polysemantic, runs opposite to the essay, but it is cited from Olah et al. rather than measured. The dense versus MoE probe gap could interest V2 only as indirect, confounded evidence: it uses best-of-many selection, only personalization concepts, and dense comparators that differ in training recipe. It is not counted as a test.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or estimate the shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.

Tests personalization-related polysemanticity in three MoE models against dense comparators, but not the claimed pole-share percentages, general language-wide interpretability, or models up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose explanation, or recursive-generalization analysis.
No InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates, and no test attributing changes in interpretability shares to architecture, regularization, or tools.
Does not test attribution graphs built from the model's own neurons without a trained replacement model.
Automated explanations are for crosscoder latents rather than neuron explanations; the study does not test whether neuron explanations based on activating examples fail to predict neuron firing.
Automated scoring is applied to crosscoder-latent explanations, not neuron explanations, and does not report the share of neurons attaining a good score.

reader_labels.condition: Personalization-concept probes in the three tested MoE models versus matched-active-parameter dense models, especially at k = 1
reader_labels.reason: The authors report higher k-sparse balanced accuracy for MoEs than dense comparators, with the advantage remaining at k = 1; see r1–r3.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The study's tested personalization task and probe setup
reader_labels.reason: The results concern 20 token-labelled personalization concepts and selected best-performing components, not the fraction of neuron poles with a single job across general language use; probe label noise and selection effects are noted by the authors. See r1–r3.
